title: 7/28/2026 | CITY OF EL PASO | COM | Informal Comments of Renard U. Johnson, Mayor of the City of El Paso, in Response to Governor Greg Abbott's June 10, 2026 Data Center Directive

documents.text:
=== Response Letter - Governor Greg Abbott's (June 10th) Letter.pdf ===
RENARD U. JOHNSON

MAYOR OF EL PASO
July 27, 2026

Public Utility Commission of Texas
Central Records

1701 N. Congress Avenue

Austin, TX 78701

PROJECT NO. 58317
IMPLEMENTATION OF SENATE BILL 6

INFORMAL COMMENTS OF THE CITY OF EL PASO, TEXAS, IN RESPONSE TO
GOVERNOR GREG ABBOTT’S JUNE 10, 2026 LETTER

Executive Summary

The Governor has directed the Public Utility Commission (“Commission”) to protect Texans as
data centers grow: data centers must pay their own way, and residential electric bills must not rise
because of them. The City of El Paso (“City”) supports that directive and files these comments to
make one request: those protections should reach all Texans, including the nearly 700,000 El
Pasoans served by El Paso Electric Company outside the ERCOT grid. Data center growth in El
Paso is among the most concentrated in Texas relative to the size of the local system, yet every
protection now being developed seems to be limited to ERCOT. The City asks the Commission to
confirm that the Governor’s directive applies statewide and to open a parallel project where El
Paso and the other non-ERCOT regions can help shape protections that fit their different regulatory
framework.

I, Introduction and Statement of Support

The City appreciates the opportunity to comment on Governor Abbott’s June 10, 2026 letter and
the Commission’s July 17, 2026 response. The City fully supports the Governor’s directives: data
centers should pay for the infrastructure built to serve them; residential customers should benefit
from this growth, not pay for it; and reliability and local communities must come first. The City
also commends the Commission and its Staff for the speed and care of their work implementing
Senate Bill 6.

City of El Paso « 300N.Campbell « El Paso, TX 79901
(915) 212-0021

 RENARD U. JOHNSON

MAYOR OF EL PASO

The City raises one concern. Senate Bill 6 applies only to the ERCOT region, and the Governor’s
letter was filed in this project because the subjects overlap. But the directive itself protects Texans
without any geographic limit. El Paso lies outside ERCOT. The City asks that the protections now
being developed include El Paso and the other non-ERCOT areas of the state.

On June 23, 2026, the El Paso City Council approved amending the City’s 90th Legislative Session
State Legislative Agenda to support policies protecting residential ratepayers from utility costs
attributable to data centers and to advocate for inclusion of the electric grid serving El Paso
residents within the protections contemplated by the Governor’s June 10, 2026 directive. These
comments are consistent with the City’s formally adopted position that El Paso residents should
receive the same ratepayer, infrastructure-cost, and reliability protections being developed for
customers within ERCOT.

II. Data Center Growth in El Paso Is as Significant as Anywhere in Texas

El Paso’s nearly 700,000 residents are served by El Paso Electric Company (“EPE”), a traditional,
fully regulated utility. El Paso has welcomed responsible data center investment, and that
investment is arriving at remarkable scale:

e Meta is building a hyperscale data center in northeast El Paso (named Wurldwide LLC in
Commission filings). It is expected to begin taking power this year and to grow to a peak
demand of about 1,000 MW, one full gigawatt. In ERCOT, a load that size would be
roughly one percent of the system peak; on EPE’s system, this single customer approaches
half of the utility’s entire Texas peak demand. (Docket No. 59611.)

e More is coming. EPE itself has told the Commission that it expects to begin serving
between | and 2 GW of new load” under its proposed large-load tariff in the next 3 years,
and that load equal to half its Texas peak can materialize in a matter of a few years. (Docket
No. 59611, Direct Testimony of James Schicht! at 5-6.)

(915) 212-0021

RENARD U. JOHNSON

MAYOR OF EL PASO

e New infrastructure is already being built. EPE is seeking Commission approval to build
the McCloud Generation Facility, a roughly 366 MW power plant costing well over $400
million, specifically to serve the Meta data center. (Docket No. 59076.) The City is a party
in that case, working to ensure that a plant built for one customer is paid for by that
customer, not by El Paso’s families and small businesses. That is exactly the outcome the
Governor has directed.

Because EPE’s system is a small fraction of ERCOT’s size, each of these risks weighs more
heavily on each El Paso ratepayer.

III. The Governor’s Directive Reaches All Texans

The Governor directed the PUCT, whose jurisdiction covers the entire state, to make sure data
centers pay all of their own infrastructure costs so that “no residential ratepayer is burdened by
those costs,” and to use its “existing authorities” to “safeguard Texans, their property, and
resources.” Nothing in the directive limits those protections to ERCOT, and the Commission’s
existing authority includes full ratemaking and certification jurisdiction over the utilities outside
ERCOT.

The City understands why the work so far has centered on ERCOT: Senate Bill 6 requires it, and
the Commission’s SB 6 rulemakings are properly limited to that region. The City objects to none
of that work. The concern is what is missing: there is no companion effort for the parts of Texas
outside ERCOT, even though some of the most concentrated data center growth in the state is
happening there. El Pasoans are the “everyday Texans” the Governor’s letter is written to protect.

IV. The City’s Proposals

The non-ERCOT regions operate under a different framework. EPE is a bundled, cost-of-service
utility: it owns its power plants and wires, and its rates are set by regulators, including cities like
El! Paso that hold original rate jurisdiction, rather than by a competitive market. Rules written for
ERCOT’s competitive market cannot simply be copied over; the protections must be tailored. The
City therefore respectfully requests that the Commission:

Public Utility Commission of Texas July 27, 2026 Page 3

City of El Paso + 300N.Campbell + El Paso, TX 79901
(915) 212-0021

 V.

RENARD U. JOHNSON

MAYOR OF EL PASO

. Confirm that the protections developed in response to the Governor’s letter will extend to

all of Texas, including the areas outside ERCOT.

. Open a separate, parallel rulemaking or project addressing large-load growth in the non-

ERCOT regions, so that utilities, cities, consumer representatives, and other stakeholders
have a dedicated venue to propose protections that fit the cost-of-service framework. The
City stands ready to participate constructively.

In the meantime, apply the principles of the Governor’s directive in pending and future
cases involving non-ERCOT utilities, including EPE’s large-load tariff case (Docket No.
59611) and its pending certification cases (Docket Nos. 59076, 59585, 59690, 59836,
59899, and 60016).

Ensure that any legislation the Commission recommends to the Legislature covers large
loads statewide, so that the millions of Texans served outside ERCOT, in far West Texas,
the Panhandle, and East Texas, receive the same safeguards as their fellow citizens.

Conclusion

EI Paso shares the Governor’s vision: welcome the investment, and protect the people. The City is
grateful to the Governor for his directives and to the Commission for its diligent work, and asks
only that the protections now taking shape be built for all Texans, including the residents of El
Paso. The City stands ready to help in any way it can.

Sincerely,

fit

Renard U. Johnson
Mayor
